appraisal_events.evidence: Charlus ranks the Cambremer with « tous les petits messieurs qui s'appellent marquis de Cambremerde », between whom and « le dernier pioupiou de votre régiment » there is « aucune différence » ; Morel, his instrument, leaves the invitation unanswered and excuses himself by telegram, and at the dinner staged to exhibit the baron to the Férés « la porte s'ouvrit et Mme de Cambremer faillit se trouver mal en voyant Morel entrer seul ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The dominant movement of the passage is a sustained social snub of the Cambremer, doctrinally authorized by Charlus and executed through Morel, which collapses precisely the dinner Mme de Cambremer had staged to display the baron to the socially unassailable Férés. The narrator's own framing of the Cambremer as timid, naive and routine-bound (« par une fausse appréciation de l'élégance », « cela ne bicherait pas ») endorses their deflation even while mocking Charlus's coarse manner of stating it.

appraisal_events.evidence: Refusing to walk a hundred metres to greet Bloch's father while Saint-Loup sits beside Albertine, the narrator is judged by Bloch, who « ne douta pas que ce fût parce que décidément [...] j'étais snob » ; « De ce jour il cessa de me témoigner la même amitié, et, ce qui m'était plus pénible, n'eut plus pour mon caractère la même estime. »
appraisal_events.explanation: Bloch's blame durably lowers the narrator's standing in his eyes and destroys the friendship. The narration ironizes the charge — the imputed snobbery is a « tort imaginaire », the real motive being jealousy of Albertine — yet concedes both that the loss is real and that the true explanation would be still less creditable.

status_effects.explanation: The chemist's smile with which she anticipated introducing Charlus to Mme Féré turns into near-collapse when Morel enters alone; her Féterne evening, her leverage over the little clan and her claim to command a great name all fail publicly at once.

He shares the rebuff and his retaliation — attending la Raspelière alone as though a princess of the blood conducting a duchess only halfway — is narrated as a petty, provincial gesture that formalizes the break without recovering standing.

Both parties defer to him: the Cambremer's belated climb-down « fit sourire M. de Charlus en lui montrant son pouvoir », and his mere absence is enough to ruin their evening, though the narrator simultaneously calls him « insupportable, tatillon, et même, lui si fin, bête » in such moods.

He wins the exchange practically but is lowered in the telling: he receives Charlus's crude genealogy « pieusement », judges as if he were himself a Guermantes, and snubs the Cambremer « ravi comme s'il venait d'agir en prince du sang », a literal application the narrator calls « burlesque ».

In Bloch's eyes he is fixed as a snob who behaves differently before « des gens nés », and loses both the friendship and, more painfully, Bloch's esteem for his character, with no correction available to him.

ambiguities: The Féterne dinner's humiliated hostess is designated only as « Mme de Cambremer » / « la marquise », a surface form the registry treats as shared with the dowager marquise; it is read here as the younger marquise (née Legrandin), since she is the one who consults the narrator about inviting Mme Verdurin, who blushes over Morel, and who had met the Férés through M. de Chevrigny, while the dowager is separately marked « la vieille marquise ».
